mstts:express-as.prosody: Let’s talk about something that’s shaped so much of the world we know today—colonization. Now, when you hear that word, maybe you picture ships arriving on distant shores, explorers planting flags, or treaties being signed under pressure. But for the people who actually lived through it, colonization wasn’t just a chapter in a textbook. It was something they felt every single day, changing the way they lived, the rules they followed, and even how they saw themselves. Imagine a parent watching as their village is suddenly expected to follow new laws, speak a different language, and let go of traditions passed down for generations. The change would be dizzying—overnight, children in school are taught to see their own ways as outdated, and to look up to foreign customs instead. The message was clear: if you wanted to move forward, you had to leave the old ways behind. But colonization reached far beyond just politics or government. It was deeply personal. Families were split apart, economies turned upside down, and communities found themselves divided by new borders—borders drawn by people who’d never even set foot there. Think about that for a moment: lines on a map, cutting through towns and families, creating tensions that sometimes still echo today. And if you look around, you can still see the legacy of colonization everywhere. It’s in the languages people speak, the laws they follow, and the ways they understand themselves and each other. Many challenges faced by African countries today? They’re tied directly to decisions made during the colonial era. But, here’s something important: the story of colonization isn’t just about loss. It’s also about resistance, adaptation, and survival. Across Africa, people held on to their cultures, pushed back against domination, and even found clever ways to use the colonizers’ tools for their own purposes—maybe by using a new language to spread their own ideas, or by fighting for their rights in court. Decolonization was tough. It wasn’t just about winning political freedom—it was about figuring out who you are after so much has been changed. For many, the end of colonial rule was just the start of a whole new challenge: how do you rebuild a society that’s been divided and transformed? The healing and restoration—that work is still going on, even today. If you want to make sense of why the world looks the way it does now—why some countries thrive while others struggle, why certain languages dominate, or why some histories seem to be everywhere while others are barely mentioned—understanding colonization is key. It shows us how power doesn’t just shape the past, but keeps shaping our present and future, too. And for those living in the shadow of colonization, reclaiming history is both deeply personal and deeply political. It means questioning the stories they’ve been told, searching for the voices that were silenced, and facing some uncomfortable truths. More than that, it’s about imagining new possibilities—new ways for communities to come together and move forward. Whether it’s in classrooms, around dinner tables, or within communities, the journey to decolonize history is ongoing. It’s a process of unlearning, of asking tough questions, and of building something new. Most of all, it’s about recognizing just how much the past still shapes our lives, and daring to dream of a future that celebrates the resilience and diversity of everyone.
